title: Why 'Get Rich' Gurus Sell Courses Instead of Doing It
sources: FTC press release, June 2018, 'FTC Action Halts MOBE, a Massive Internet Business Coaching Scheme': defendants allegedly took more than $125 million from thousands of consumers; $49 entry fee for a '21-step system', then membership packages costing thousands of dollars; the 'proven system' turned out to be selling the same memberships to others; most buyers could not recoup their costs, some lost more than $20,000; refunds often refused or paid only after persistent demands (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2018/06/ftc-action-halts-mobe-massive-internet-business-coaching-scheme)

FTC Business Blog, June 2018, 'FTC alleges MOBE tells a whale of a tale with misleading money-making claims': 21-Step System for $49 or less; Gold Masterclass $4,997; Diamond Mastermind $29,997; FTC: 'the primary thing MOBE sells is more MOBE memberships'; fine print: 'the average Consultant ... generates less than $250 per year'; '100% risk-free' 30-day money-back promise (ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2018/06/ftc-alleges-mobe-tells-whale-tale-misleading-money-making-claims)

FTC press release, Oct 2019, 'FTC Acts Against Company Using Celebrity Endorsements, Bogus Earnings Claims to Sell Real Estate Seminars' (Zurixx, with Utah Division of Consumer Protection): free event was a sales pitch for a $1,997 three-day workshop, described as 'beginner' level; upsells cost as much as $41,297; presenters routinely told attendees to get new credit cards or raise credit limits; some refund recipients had to sign agreements barring them from speaking with the FTC (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/10/ftc-acts-against-company-using-celebrity-endorsements-bogus-earnings-claims-sell-real-estate)

FTC press release, July 2024, 'FTC Sends More Than $12 Million in Refunds to Consumers Harmed by Zurixx': more than $12 million to 25,563 consumers; February 2022 settlement permanently banned the defendants from selling real estate or business coaching programs (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/07/ftc-sends-more-12-million-refunds-consumers-harmed-zurixx-real-estate-investment-coaching-scheme)

FTC press release, 26 Oct 2021, 'FTC Puts Businesses on Notice that False Money-Making Claims Could Lead to Big Penalties': Notice of Penalty Offenses sent to more than 1,100 businesses including business coaching; listed deceptive practices include misrepresenting earnings, claiming profits are typical, claiming no experience is needed, and claiming consumers must act immediately

FTC press release, 13 Jan 2025, 'FTC Proposes Rule Changes and New Rule to Deter Deceptive Earnings Claims by Multilevel Marketers and Money-Making Opportunity Sellers': proposal (3-2 vote) to extend the Business Opportunity Rule (16 CFR 437) to money-making opportunities such as business coaching; sellers would need written substantiation for earnings claims; deceptive earnings claims are already illegal

PBS American Experience, 'The Gold Rush' (film and companion features): Sam Brannan waved a vial of gold through San Francisco shouting 'Gold! Gold from the American River!' after stocking up on prospecting supplies; sales at his store near the mines totaled $36,000 in May, June and early July 1848; he never mined, and became California's first millionaire; most miners did hard labor and many ended up as wage workers
FTC ReportFraud portal: reportfraud.ftc.gov (where consumers report money-making scams)
Illustrative math (story, not a statistic): $1,997 x 1,000 buyers = $1,997,000 in revenue for one recorded workshop. Dave, Kevin, the guru and the coach are fictional characters.

FTC Notice of Penalty Offenses Concerning Money-Making Opportunities (Oct 2021)
FTC proposed Earnings Claim Rule for business opportunities and coaching (2025)
Sam Brannan and the 1848 Gold Rush (California State Library)

youtube.title: Why 'Get Rich' Gurus Sell You Courses Instead of Doing It
alt_titles: You Paid $1,997 for His System. Why Is He Selling It?
Why Your 'Free Training' Always Ends With an Upsell
youtube.hook: It's 2 AM and Dave is about to pay $9,997 for a course on getting rich. If the system really works, why is the guru selling it instead of using it? Dave joins a free webinar, buys a $1,997 'beginner' workshop, and is one click away from the $9,997 Platinum level. We follow the upsell ladder step by step, using what the FTC found in real cases: one program took more than $125 million while its average member made under $250 a year, and another pushed upsells as high as $41,297. Then the 1848 gold rush shopkeeper who got rich without digging, why the refund guarantee turns into a maze, and the one question that made the sales coach hang up.
youtube.pinned: Have you ever bought a course that promised to make you rich? What happened? (No judgment, Dave almost paid $9,997.)

beats.text: This is me at two in the morning about to pay nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars for a course on how to get rich.
And the guy selling it lives in a mansion so obviously he knows the secret right?
Spoiler.
By the end of this video you'll know the one question that made his coach hang up on me in four seconds and you can use it on any guru.
But most people click off before that part which is exactly what the gurus want.
So it starts like this. An ad pops up that says free training and ninety minutes that will change your life. I grab a snack and I click.
I'm a very smart person so I wrote down my goal in a notebook. Get rich. That was the whole plan.
Minute one he shows me his mansion. Minute ten it's his car. Minute forty he's on a jet ski.
Me watching a stranger's jet ski for forty minutes like it's a documentary.
Minute sixty I'm still waiting for the part where I get rich.
Minute eighty five and there's still no secret but there is an offer. A three day workshop for one thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars with only twenty spots and a countdown timer.
It's like a free sample at the grocery store except the guy with the toothpick follows you all the way to the checkout.
I watch the spots drop. Nineteen. Eighteen. Seventeen. And I buy one.
Me pressing the buy button.
And on day one of the workshop I hear a sentence I'm going to hear again and again. This is just the beginner level.
Spoiler again. It's always the beginner level.
Day one I fill a whole notebook with excitement and almost zero actual steps.
Day two the guru explains that the real system lives in the advanced program. There's Gold and there's Platinum and there's Diamond.
It's like a game that's free to download. Then the sword costs money and then the armor and then the horse and somehow you never reach the castle.
And the worst part is that every level comes with the same promise. This is the one that finally works. The next level is where the real money is. Trust me bro.
My wallet climbing the guru ladder.
And this isn't something I made up. The FTC sued a real coaching company called Zurixx that did this exact thing with a free event then a three day workshop then the upsells.
Quick guess before I tell you. How high do you think that ladder went? Write your number in the comments.

Back at the workshop a coach pulls me aside and whispers Platinum. Nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars. And if my credit limit is too low I should just call my card company and ask for more.
Be honest. You've been one click away from something like this at two in the morning.
I had one night to decide. So I did the one thing the guru never taught me. I looked him up.
Me at the workshop versus me after one Google search.
That mansion from the video? It's a vacation rental. You can book it for the night.
I scrolled through the photos and there it was. The same pool and the same couch and the same fancy kitchen. Forty two five star reviews. One of them said great place for filming.
The guru when I found the rental listing.
Then I looked for his million dollar business and I found exactly one business. The course.
And that reminded me of a crazy story from eighteen forty eight in San Francisco.
A shopkeeper named Sam Brannan runs through the streets waving a little bottle of gold and shouting gold from the American River.
Thousands of people rush off to dig. But Sam had already bought every pick and pan and shovel he could find and his store sold them like crazy.
Most miners got blisters. Sam became California's first millionaire. And he never dug for gold.
Sam Brannan explaining the business model to the miners.
Oh and the answer to the guess. In the Zurixx case the ladder went up to forty one thousand dollars. For coaching.
So I asked myself the scary question. What if the course isn't how he got rich? What if the course is the gold?
Then I found the biggest one. A program called MOBE that the FTC says took over one hundred twenty five million dollars from people.
It started at forty nine dollars and then the masterclasses went up to almost thirty thousand.
And the proven system for making money? According to the FTC it was mostly selling more memberships to other people.
So the people at the top got rich from the people at the bottom who were promised they'd get rich from the people below them. And at the very bottom there's just a guy like me with a notebook.
It's like a restaurant where the only thing on the menu is a recipe for opening a restaurant.
The guru economy explained.
And the fine print? The average member made less than two hundred fifty dollars a year and some people lost more than twenty thousand.
So the villain isn't one guy in a mansion. It's the machine behind him. A sales funnel built to move you up one more step again and again.
But that left me with a weird question. If someone really had a money machine why would they sell it at all?
My brain trying to understand the guru business.
Think about my uncle's secret fishing spot. It's full of fish and he has never told a single person where it is.
Because if he sold a map to a thousand people that spot would be empty by Tuesday.
My uncle if you ask him where the spot is.
Real money tricks work the same way. The more people use them the less they work. So a real secret gets kept and not sold.
But a course is different. You record it once and you sell it forever with no shop and no stock and no risk.
Sell a two thousand dollar workshop to a thousand people and that's almost two million dollars even if nobody in the room ever gets rich.
Him counting our money while we take notes.
I used to think he's rich so he must know the secret. Nope. He's rich because people like me believed he knew the secret.
So I decided to get my money back. That's when things got worse.
I email support. The sales page promised one hundred percent risk free and a thirty day money back guarantee.
Reply one says fill out the form. Reply two says first you must finish every lesson. Reply three says nothing.
It's like pushing a revolving door. Lots of effort and you end up exactly where you started.
Me after reply number three.
And it wasn't just me. The FTC says MOBE often refused refunds and in the Zurixx case some people had to sign a paper promising not to talk to the FTC.
Customer support in the guru world.
Then my workshop buddy Kevin texts me. He bought Platinum on two credit cards and his coach has the perfect fix. Buy the next level.
And I'm staring at my own Platinum offer. Still open. Two spots left. Maybe I have to spend more to win it all back?

And honestly that's the moment the whole trap is built for. When you're down two thousand dollars the only thing that feels like hope is spending ten thousand more. Casinos do it and guru funnels do it and they both call it an opportunity.
Yeah no.
Because there's one thing these gurus really don't want you to know and it's sitting right there in the rules.
So I open the FTC website. Quick reminder this is education and not advice.
Clue one. Lying about how much you'll earn is already illegal and in twenty twenty one the FTC warned more than eleven hundred companies about it.
Clue two. The warning even lists the tricks. Saying the results are typical. Saying you don't need experience. Saying you must act right now.
My countdown timer suddenly looked very different.
Clue three. In twenty twenty five the FTC proposed rules aimed right at business coaching where any money promise needs written proof.
So I made a plan. I saved screenshots of every promise and I reported the program and I called my card company about disputing the charge.
And the Platinum offer? I closed the tab. Nine thousand nine hundred ninety seven dollars saved.
The FTC after I sent my screenshots.
But I still had one call booked with my enrollment coach. And this time I prepared a question.
He picks up all smiles. So Dave. Ready for Platinum?
And I say maybe. But one question first. What did your typical student earn last year after paying for the program? And can you send that in writing?
Silence. Then well results vary. Then oh I have another call. Click.
Four seconds. I timed it.
That's the question. Not how much did you make. How much did your typical buyer make. In writing.
Because the guru's real number was never his income. It was how many people like me bought the course.
A guy with a real money machine doesn't need your two thousand dollars. A guy selling one does.
Gurus when you ask for proof in writing.
So do gurus get rich from their secret?
beats.card: Do gurus get rich from their secret?

beats.text: No. They get rich from yours.
So here's what I learned. If someone sells the secret then the selling is the business.
Free training is just the first step of a very long and very expensive ladder.
And always ask what the typical buyer earned. In writing.
And if a timer is counting down while someone is talking about your future close the tab. Real opportunities don't disappear in eleven minutes.
A week later my friend Bob knocks on my door with a business opportunity and he swears it is not a pyramid.
Subscribe so I can find out if Bob is lying. He's lying.
